summary_html: The **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** created a national commission to study child-fatality prevention. Project Milk Carton cross-references its findings with state fatality data to expose non-implementation.

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: In re Fortieth Statewide Investigating Grand Jury
key_cases.holding: The court ordered interim release of the clergy-abuse grand jury report with the challengers' identities redacted, holding that Pennsylvania's constitutional right to reputation requires enhanced procedural protections before a grand jury report publicly condemns named individuals.
key_cases.relevance: The Pennsylvania model for a public fatality- or abuse-review report and the process due before release.
key_cases.quote: the lines between a grand jury "investigation" and an "adjudication" are blurred when the grand jury renders wide-scale, individualized, condemnatory findings

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed, holding that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative constitutional duty on a child-protection agency to protect a child from private violence where the child remains in the parent's custody rather than in state custody.
key_cases.relevance: Frames why fatality review is a policy and oversight function, not a constitutional remedy.
key_cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court held that placing a child in state-regulated foster care creates a special relationship imposing affirmative constitutional duties, but affirmed summary judgment because the caseworker's conduct amounted at most to negligence and did not shock the conscience.
key_cases.relevance: Explains why deaths and serious injuries in care raise constitutional, not merely administrative, questions.
key_cases.quote: when the state places a child in state-regulated foster care, the state has entered into a special relationship with that child which imposes upon it certain affirmative duties
